title: Climate Change
description: The greenhouse effect, the evidence that our climate is changing, the causes and impacts, and how the world is responding.

notes.heading: 📌 The Natural Greenhouse Effect
notes.body: The greenhouse effect is a natural process that makes life on Earth possible. Energy from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface. The warm surface then gives off heat (infrared radiation) back towards space. Greenhouse gases in the atmosphere — carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), water vapour and nitrous oxide — absorb some of this outgoing heat and re-radiate it in all directions, warming the lower atmosphere. It works a little like the glass of a greenhouse or a blanket around the planet. Without any greenhouse effect, the average temperature of the Earth would be about minus 18 degrees C and the oceans would freeze. With the natural greenhouse effect, the average is a comfortable 15 degrees C. The problem is not the greenhouse effect itself — it is that humans are strengthening it.

notes.heading: 🔑 The Enhanced Greenhouse Effect
notes.body: Since the Industrial Revolution (around 1750), human activities have been adding extra greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, thickening the blanket and trapping more heat — this is the enhanced greenhouse effect, which causes global warming and climate change. Global average temperature has risen by roughly 1.1-1.2 degrees C since pre-industrial times. That may sound small, but even a degree or two shifts climate zones, melts ice and raises sea levels. Climate change does not mean everywhere simply gets hotter: it means the whole climate system becomes more energetic and less predictable — some places get more extreme rainfall and flooding, others get worse droughts and heatwaves, and storms can intensify. The term global warming describes the rising temperature; climate change describes all the resulting shifts in weather patterns.

notes.heading: 📎 The Evidence for Climate Change
notes.body: Scientists use many independent lines of evidence. Ice cores: drilling into the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets extracts cores containing air bubbles trapped up to 800,000 years ago. These show that CO2 levels and temperature have always risen and fallen together — and that CO2 is now higher (over 420 parts per million) than at any time in that entire record. Temperature records: thermometers have measured global temperature directly since about 1850, and the ten warmest years on record have all occurred recently. Sea level: tide gauges and satellites show global sea level has risen about 20 cm since 1900 and the rate is speeding up. Other evidence includes retreating glaciers and shrinking Arctic sea ice (measured by satellite since 1979), oceans becoming more acidic as they absorb CO2, and spring arriving earlier. Each line of evidence points the same way, which is why scientists are confident the climate is changing and humans are the main cause.

notes.heading: 🔑 The Causes: Where Greenhouse Gases Come From
notes.body: Burning fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — for electricity, heating, industry and transport is the biggest cause, releasing CO2 that was locked underground for millions of years. Deforestation makes things worse twice over: burning or rotting trees releases stored carbon, and fewer trees remain to absorb CO2. Agriculture is a major source of other gases: cattle and sheep belch methane (a gas over 80 times more powerful than CO2 in the short term), rice paddies release methane, and fertilisers release nitrous oxide. Other contributors include cement production, landfill sites (rotting rubbish releases methane) and air travel. A person's or country's carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas emissions caused by their activities. Richer countries generally have much larger footprints per person, though fast-industrialising countries now have the largest totals.

notes.heading: ⚠️ The Impacts of Climate Change
notes.body: Climate change affects weather, oceans, ecosystems and people. Extreme weather: heatwaves, droughts, wildfires, intense rainfall and floods are becoming more frequent or severe in many regions, and warmer oceans can fuel stronger tropical storms. Sea-level rise: oceans rise partly because warmer water expands (thermal expansion) and partly because melting glaciers and ice sheets add water — threatening low-lying coasts, delta cities and island nations such as the Maldives and Tuvalu. Ecosystems: coral reefs suffer bleaching when water gets too warm, species are shifting towards the poles, and those that cannot move (like polar bears on shrinking sea ice) decline. People: harvests and water supplies become less reliable (threatening food and water security), heat stress and diseases spread, and millions may be displaced by floods, drought or rising seas — climate refugees. The impacts fall hardest on poorer countries that contributed least to the problem.

notes.heading: 💡 Mitigation versus Adaptation
notes.body: Responses to climate change fall into two categories, and we need both. Mitigation means tackling the causes — reducing greenhouse gas emissions to limit how much warming happens. Examples: switching from fossil fuels to renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro), improving energy efficiency, electric transport, carbon capture and storage, protecting and replanting forests, and eating less meat. Adaptation means coping with the effects that are already unavoidable — adjusting how we live to the changes underway. Examples: building sea walls and flood defences, developing drought-resistant crops, storing more water, designing cities with shade and green space to stay cool, early-warning systems for storms and heatwaves, and managed retreat from the most threatened coasts. A good way to remember the difference: mitigation avoids the unmanageable; adaptation manages the unavoidable.

notes.heading: 🔑 Taking Action: Individuals, Governments and the World
notes.body: Climate change must be tackled at every scale. Individuals can walk, cycle or use public transport, save energy at home, eat less meat, waste less food, and reduce, reuse and recycle — small actions that add up across millions of people. National governments can set legal targets (many countries aim for net zero emissions by 2050), tax carbon, subsidise renewable energy and electric vehicles, ban petrol car sales, and fund adaptation such as flood defences. International action is essential because the atmosphere belongs to no one: the 1997 Kyoto Protocol was the first major treaty to cut emissions, and the 2015 Paris Agreement committed nearly every country to keeping warming well below 2 degrees C, with efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees C. Progress is reviewed at annual COP conferences. A key tension is fairness: poorer countries argue they should not have to sacrifice development for a problem mostly created by rich countries, so the Paris Agreement includes funding to help them cut emissions and adapt.

flashcards.definition: The natural process by which gases in the atmosphere trap heat radiated from the Earth's surface, keeping the planet warm enough for life.
flashcards.example: Without the natural greenhouse effect, average global temperature would be about minus 18 degrees C instead of 15 degrees C.

flashcards.definition: A gas that absorbs outgoing heat and warms the atmosphere — mainly carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour and nitrous oxide.
flashcards.example: CO2 from burning fossil fuels and methane from cattle are both powerful greenhouse gases.

flashcards.definition: The strengthening of the natural greenhouse effect caused by humans adding extra greenhouse gases, leading to global warming.
flashcards.example: Global average temperature has risen by over 1 degree C since pre-industrial times.

flashcards.definition: A cylinder of ice drilled from an ice sheet, containing air bubbles that reveal past atmospheric CO2 levels and temperatures over hundreds of thousands of years.
flashcards.example: Antarctic ice cores show CO2 is now higher than at any point in the last 800,000 years.

flashcards.definition: Coal, oil and natural gas — fuels formed from ancient organisms, which release CO2 when burned for energy.
flashcards.example: Power stations, cars and heating systems burning fossil fuels are the biggest source of human CO2 emissions.

flashcards.definition: The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by the activities of a person, organisation or country.
flashcards.example: Flying abroad on holiday and eating a lot of beef both increase your carbon footprint.

flashcards.definition: The increase in volume of ocean water as it warms — one of the two main causes of sea-level rise, alongside melting land ice.
flashcards.example: Even if no ice melted at all, warming oceans would still make sea levels rise through thermal expansion.

flashcards.definition: The whitening of coral reefs when overly warm water forces corals to expel the algae they depend on, which can kill the reef.
flashcards.example: Marine heatwaves have repeatedly bleached large parts of the Great Barrier Reef.

flashcards.definition: Action to reduce the causes of climate change by cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
flashcards.example: Replacing a coal power station with a wind farm is mitigation.

flashcards.definition: Action to cope with the effects of climate change that are already happening or unavoidable.
flashcards.example: Building a sea wall to protect a coastal town from rising seas is adaptation.

flashcards.definition: The 2015 international treaty committing nearly every country to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees C, with efforts towards 1.5 degrees C.
flashcards.example: Progress on the Paris Agreement is reviewed at annual COP climate conferences.

flashcards.definition: A balance where any greenhouse gases emitted are matched by an equal amount removed from the atmosphere, so net emissions are zero.
flashcards.example: Many countries have set legal targets to reach net zero emissions by 2050.

questions.stem: What is the natural greenhouse effect?
choices: A hole in the atmosphere that lets heat in
Gases in the atmosphere trapping heat radiated from the Earth's surface, keeping the planet warm enough for life
The Sun heating the inside of glass buildings
Forests absorbing all carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb some of the heat the warm Earth radiates towards space and re-radiate it back, raising the average temperature from about minus 18 to 15 degrees C. Without it, Earth would be frozen.

questions.stem: Which of these is a major greenhouse gas released by cattle and rice farming?
choices: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Methane
Argon
questions.explanation: Cattle and sheep release methane when they digest food, and flooded rice paddies produce it too. Methane traps far more heat per molecule than CO2 in the short term.

questions.stem: How do ice cores provide evidence about past climate?
choices: They contain fossils of warm-weather animals
Air bubbles trapped in the ice reveal CO2 levels and temperatures going back 800,000 years
They show how thick the ice was in each century
They contain tree rings from ancient forests
questions.explanation: Each layer of ice traps tiny bubbles of the atmosphere from when the snow fell. Analysing them shows CO2 and temperature moving together — and that CO2 is now higher than at any time in 800,000 years.

questions.stem: Why is sea level rising as the climate warms?
choices: Only because melting land ice adds water to the oceans
Only because warm water expands
Because warmer ocean water expands AND melting glaciers and ice sheets add extra water
Because increased rainfall flows into the sea
questions.explanation: Sea-level rise has two main drivers: thermal expansion (warm water takes up more space) and meltwater from land-based glaciers and ice sheets. Melting sea ice adds little because it already floats.

questions.stem: Which human activity is the single biggest source of CO2 emissions?
choices: Burning fossil fuels for energy, industry and transport
Farming cattle
Using aerosol sprays
Building houses from wood
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas for electricity, heating, industry and transport releases more CO2 than any other human activity, which is why switching to renewable energy is central to tackling climate change.

questions.stem: How does deforestation worsen climate change?
choices: Trees give off heat when cut down
Burning or rotting trees release stored carbon, and fewer trees remain to absorb CO2
Tree roots release methane when exposed to air
Open land creates more clouds that trap heat
questions.explanation: Forests store vast amounts of carbon in their wood and leaves. Clearing them releases that carbon into the atmosphere while also removing one of the planet's main natural absorbers of CO2.

choices: Corals grow faster in warm water
Overly warm water forces corals to expel the algae they depend on, turning them white and often killing them
Pollution paints the coral white
Corals change colour to attract fish
questions.explanation: Corals live in partnership with tiny algae that provide most of their food. When water gets too warm, corals expel the algae, lose their colour and food supply, and may die if the heat persists.

questions.stem: A country builds a sea wall to protect a coastal city from rising seas. Is this mitigation or adaptation?
choices: Mitigation — it reduces emissions
Adaptation — it copes with an effect of climate change rather than tackling the cause
Neither — sea walls are unrelated to climate change
Both equally
questions.explanation: Adaptation means adjusting to effects already underway, like sea-level rise. The sea wall does not cut any emissions; mitigation would mean measures like renewable energy that reduce the warming itself.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of climate change MITIGATION?
choices: Developing drought-resistant crops
Installing early-warning systems for heatwaves
Replacing a coal-fired power station with solar farms
Moving a village away from a flooding coastline
questions.explanation: Mitigation tackles the causes by cutting emissions — solar farms replace fossil-fuel electricity. Drought-resistant crops, warning systems and relocating villages all help people cope with effects, so they are adaptation.

questions.stem: Why do poorer countries often argue that international climate agreements are unfair to them?
choices: They are not allowed to attend COP conferences
They contributed least to historical emissions but suffer the worst impacts, and cutting emissions could slow their development
Their climates are not changing
They produce more greenhouse gases than rich countries per person
questions.explanation: Rich countries industrialised first and caused most of the accumulated emissions, yet the harshest impacts — drought, flooding, sea-level rise — often hit poorer nations hardest. Agreements like Paris include funding to help them cut emissions without sacrificing development.

questions.stem: What was the main goal of the 2015 Paris Agreement?
choices: To ban all fossil fuels immediately worldwide
To keep global warming well below 2 degrees C, with efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees C
To plant one trillion trees
To create the first ever climate treaty
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement committed nearly every country to holding warming well below 2 degrees C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing 1.5 degrees C. The first major treaty was Kyoto in 1997, not Paris.

questions.stem: Why does a global temperature rise of only 1-2 degrees C matter so much?
choices: It does not — 2 degrees is too small to notice
It is a global average that shifts entire climate zones, melts ice, raises seas and makes extreme weather more frequent and severe
It only affects the polar regions
It doubles the length of summer everywhere
questions.explanation: A small rise in the GLOBAL average represents an enormous amount of extra energy in the climate system. It shifts climate zones, melts ice sheets, raises sea levels and loads the dice towards more heatwaves, floods and intense storms.

questions.stem: Which combination of evidence gives scientists confidence that recent warming is caused by humans?
choices: A single hot summer in one country
Multiple independent records — thermometer data since 1850, ice cores, rising seas, retreating glaciers — all pointing the same way, alongside rising CO2 from human activity
Ancient cave paintings showing hot weather
The fact that weather varies from year to year
questions.explanation: Confidence comes from many independent lines of evidence agreeing: direct temperature records, ice-core CO2, sea-level rise, glacier retreat and ocean acidification, all matching what physics predicts from human emissions.

questions.stem: Which personal action would most reduce an individual's carbon footprint?
choices: Recycling a plastic bottle once a week
Switching from driving alone to cycling or public transport and eating less meat
Buying bottled water instead of using the tap
Leaving devices on standby instead of switching them off
questions.explanation: Transport and diet (especially red meat) are among the largest parts of a personal footprint. Recycling helps, but cutting car use and meat consumption saves far more emissions.

questions.stem: A low-lying island nation cannot stop its land from flooding even if global emissions fall, because warming already in the system will raise seas for decades. What does this situation best illustrate?
choices: That mitigation is pointless
That adaptation is necessary alongside mitigation, because some climate change is already locked in
That islands should increase their emissions
That sea-level rise only affects rich countries
questions.explanation: Past emissions commit the planet to further warming and sea-level rise whatever we do next, so vulnerable places must adapt (sea walls, raised buildings, relocation) at the same time as the world mitigates to stop things getting worse.
